conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is uveitis and which is the commonest form?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Inflammation of the uveal tract (the pigmented middle layer — iris, ciliary body, choroid). Anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis — inflammation of the iris ± ciliary body) is the commonest form (~75%).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: Why does anterior uveitis matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: It is a leading cause of the painful red eye with photophobia, the classic HLA-B27/seronegative spondyloarthropathy eye disease (a major rheumatology crossover), it recurs, and untreated it causes sight-threatening complications (posterior synechiae, glaucoma, cataract, macular oedema).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What makes up the uvea, and how is uveitis classified by site?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: The uvea = iris + ciliary body + choroid. Classified as anterior (iris/ciliary body), intermediate (vitreous), posterior (choroid/retina), or panuveitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the pathophysiology of the signs in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Inflammation of the anterior chamber causes breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier, so white cells and protein leak into the anterior chamber — producing the hallmark 'cells and flare'.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: How do anterior and posterior uveitis differ in presentation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Anterior (iris ± ciliary body): painful, red, photophobic; signs = anterior chamber cells/flare, KPs, hypopyon, synechiae. Posterior (choroid/retina): often painless, white eye; main symptoms = floaters and visual loss; signs = vitritis and chorioretinal lesions.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: How does acute differ from chronic anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Acute: sudden, painful, self-limiting, recurrent (classic HLA-B27 pattern). Chronic: insidious, less painful (e.g. JIA, sarcoidosis) — more dangerous because it is quiet.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are the clinical symptoms of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: A painful red eye (dull ache over hours–days), often severe photophobia (ciliary muscle spasm), excessive watering, and blurred vision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is consensual photophobia and why is it useful?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Shining light in the OTHER (unaffected) eye causes pain in the affected eye — this distinguishes anterior uveitis from conjunctivitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is ciliary flush?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Circumcorneal injection — redness concentrated around the limbus/cornea (vs the diffuse, fornix-based redness of conjunctivitis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the pupil like in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Small (miosis from iris spasm) and may be irregular if posterior synechiae have formed.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the defining slit-lamp sign of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Anterior chamber 'cells and flare' — inflammatory cells plus protein producing a hazy/'milky' beam.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are keratic precipitates (KPs)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Clumps of inflammatory cells deposited on the corneal endothelium — a slit-lamp sign of uveitis. Large 'mutton-fat' KPs suggest granulomatous causes (e.g. sarcoidosis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is a hypopyon and which causes are classic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: A layer of white cells in the anterior chamber — classic in HLA-B27-associated uveitis and Behçet's disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are posterior synechiae and their danger?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Adhesions where the iris sticks to the lens → an irregular/festooned pupil → risk of iris bombé → glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: Roughly what proportion of anterior uveitis has a systemic association?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: About 50%.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are the HLA-B27-associated causes of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Ankylosing spondylitis (commonest — young man, inflammatory back pain), reactive arthritis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'), psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease (UC/Crohn's).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What non-HLA-B27 systemic conditions are associated with uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Sarcoidosis (granulomatous — 'mutton-fat' KPs), Behçet's (uveitis + hypopyon + oral/genital ulcers), juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA — chronic, painless, ANA-positive oligoarticular children need screening), multiple sclerosis (intermediate), and infective causes (HSV/VZV, TB, syphilis, toxoplasmosis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: Why is JIA-associated uveitis particularly dangerous, and who is screened?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Because it is chronic and painless ('white' uveitis) so it goes unnoticed until complications occur — ANA-positive oligoarticular children are screened.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the classic exam stem for HLA-B27 anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: A young man with a painful, photophobic red eye + hypopyon + inflammatory back pain → HLA-B27 anterior uveitis with ankylosing spondylitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the key investigation in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Slit-lamp examination (cells/flare, KPs, hypopyon, synechiae); dilated fundoscopy for posterior involvement; and measuring IOP (uveitic glaucoma).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: When is a systemic work-up needed in anterior uveitis, and what does it include?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: A first typical mild episode often needs none. Recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, or with systemic features → investigate: HLA-B27, FBC/ESR/CRP, ACE + CXR (sarcoid), syphilis serology, TB (IGRA/CXR), ANA (JIA in children), and imaging for spondyloarthropathy — guided by history.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the first-line treatment for anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Topical corticosteroids — prednisolone acetate 1% (frequent dosing then tapered) — to suppress the inflammation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the role of a cycloplegic/mydriatic in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Cyclopentolate/atropine dilate the pupil to relieve pain (paralysing ciliary spasm) and to prevent/break posterior synechiae (keeping the iris moving off the lens).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What treatments are used for severe/posterior/resistant or chronic uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Periocular or systemic steroids for severe/posterior/resistant disease; and systemic immunosuppression/biologics (methotrexate, anti-TNF such as adalimumab) for chronic, recurrent or sight-threatening uveitis (with rheumatology).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: How is infective uveitis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Treat the underlying cause with antimicrobials — e.g. aciclovir for herpetic uveitis — and manage any associated systemic disease. Monitor and treat uveitic glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are the complications of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Posterior synechiae → irregular pupil, iris bombé → acute glaucoma; cataract (inflammation + steroid use); glaucoma (uveitic or steroid-induced); cystoid macular oedema (a common cause of visual loss); band keratopathy (chronic — calcium in the cornea); and vision loss.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is a common cause of visual loss in uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Cystoid macular oedema.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Inflammation of the outer coats of the eye — episcleritis affects the episclera (thin vascular layer between conjunctiva and sclera), and scleritis affects the sclera (tough white outer wall).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How do episcleritis and scleritis differ in seriousness?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Episcleritis is a benign, self-limiting nuisance; scleritis is a painful, sight-threatening emergency strongly linked to systemic autoimmune/vasculitic disease and can be the first sign of life-threatening granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the core clinical distinction between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Episcleritis = superficial, mild, mobile vessels that blanch, minimal/no pain, self-limiting. Scleritis = deep, severe boring pain, immobile violaceous vessels that don't blanch, systemic disease, refer urgently.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the phenylephrine (blanching) test and its results?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Apply phenylephrine (2.5–10%) drops: episcleral (superficial) vessels blanch and the eye whitens (episcleritis); scleral (deep) vessels persist/do NOT blanch (scleritis). It is the key discriminator.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How does the pain of episcleritis compare with scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Episcleritis: mild/no pain (gritty discomfort). Scleritis: severe, deep, boring pain — worse at night (wakes from sleep), worse on eye movement.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How does the redness differ between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Episcleritis: bright red/salmon-pink, sectoral. Scleritis: deep violaceous/bluish-red.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the tenderness and vessel mobility difference between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Episcleritis: not tender; superficial vessels are mobile with a cotton bud. Scleritis: globe tender to touch; deep vessels are immobile.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: Does vision differ between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Episcleritis: vision normal. Scleritis: vision may be reduced.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the systemic associations of episcleritis vs scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Episcleritis: usually idiopathic. Scleritis: ~50% have systemic autoimmune/vasculitic disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the clinical features of episcleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Acute red eye, usually sectoral (a wedge, sometimes diffuse); mild/no pain (discomfort, watering, gritty); no visual impairment, no discharge, minimal/no photophobia. Simple (diffuse/sectoral) or nodular (a mobile nodule) forms; mostly idiopathic.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How is episcleritis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Self-limiting — reassurance often all that's needed (~1–2 weeks); lubricants for comfort; topical/oral NSAIDs if troublesome; topical steroids occasionally (specialist). Investigate only if recurrent/atypical — no systemic work-up for a single typical episode.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the features of scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Severe, deep, 'boring' ocular pain radiating to brow/jaw/temple, worse at night and on eye movement (extraocular muscles insert into the sclera); globe tenderness; deep violaceous injection; may have reduced vision, photophobia, watering; often bilateral and recurrent; can involve the cornea/uvea.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: Why is scleritis pain worse on eye movement?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Because the extraocular muscles insert into the sclera.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the subtypes of ANTERIOR scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Diffuse (best prognosis); nodular (an immobile tender nodule); necrotising WITH inflammation (most severe — scleral destruction, strong vasculitis association, high morbidity/mortality); and necrotising WITHOUT inflammation (scleromalacia perforans — painless scleral thinning in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is scleromalacia perforans?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Necrotising scleritis without inflammation — painless scleral thinning in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is necrotising scleritis with inflammation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: The most severe form — scleral destruction with a strong vasculitis association and high morbidity/mortality.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is posterior scleritis and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Scleritis behind the equator, causing proptosis, pain on movement, disc swelling and retinal/choroidal changes. Harder to diagnose — needs B-scan ultrasound (the 'T-sign').

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the commonest systemic association of scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: Which vasculitis can present with scleritis and must not be missed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA/Wegener's) and other ANCA-associated vasculitides — scleritis may be the presenting feature of life-threatening vasculitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: List the systemic associations of scleritis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Rheumatoid arthritis (commonest), GPA/Wegener's and other ANCA-associated vasculitides, SLE, relapsing polychondritis, IBD, sarcoidosis, seronegative spondyloarthropathies (HLA-B27 — ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis), and infective causes (herpes zoster, TB, syphilis; gout).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What systemic work-up is done in scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: With rheumatology: FBC, ESR/CRP, U&Es + urinalysis (renal vasculitis), ANCA (GPA), RF/anti-CCP, ANA/anti-dsDNA, ACE (sarcoid), infection screen (syphilis, TB, HSV/VZV); B-scan for posterior scleritis (T-sign); CXR (sarcoid/GPA/TB).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How is scleritis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Urgent (same-day) ophthalmology referral; systemic NSAIDs (oral flurbiprofen/indomethacin — first-line for non-necrotising scleritis); systemic corticosteroids (oral ± IV pulsed) for severe/non-responsive disease; immunosuppression/biologics (methotrexate, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide or rituximab for necrotising/vasculitic disease) under rheumatology; treat the underlying systemic/infective cause; topical steroids are adjunctive.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for non-necrotising scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Systemic NSAIDs (oral flurbiprofen or indomethacin).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How does the nodule of nodular episcleritis differ from that of nodular scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: The episcleritis nodule is MOBILE; the scleritis nodule is IMMOBILE.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Separation of the neurosensory retina (photoreceptors) from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) — the light-sensing layer lifts off the tissue that nourishes it. It is a time-critical, sight-threatening emergency: the detached retina loses its blood/nutrient supply and photoreceptors die within days.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What holds the neurosensory retina and RPE together, and what happens if fluid gets between them?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: They are only loosely apposed, held together by vitreous pressure and RPE pumping. If fluid gets between them (through a tear, from traction, or by exudation), the retina detaches and photoreceptors lose RPE support and degenerate.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What are the three types of retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Rhegmatogenous (commonest — a retinal break/tear lets vitreous fluid pass under the retina); tractional (fibrous tissue pulls the retina off); and exudative/serous (fluid leaks under the retina with no break or traction).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What causes rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: A retinal break/tear lets vitreous fluid pass under the retina — associated with posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), myopia, trauma, previous cataract surgery, and lattice degeneration.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What causes tractional retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Fibrous tissue pulling the retina off — e.g. proliferative diabetic retinopathy, sickle cell disease, and prior trauma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What causes exudative (serous) retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Fluid leaking under the retina with no break and no traction — from inflammation, tumour, malignant hypertension/pre-eclampsia, or central serous retinopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What does 'rhegmatogenous' mean, and why is it important?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: From 'rhegma' (a break) — it is the classic and commonest type, presenting with flashes/floaters/curtain and needing urgent surgery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the biggest risk factor for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Myopia (short-sightedness) — a longer, thinner eye/retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the key precipitant of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) — the ageing vitreous pulls on the retina and can cause a tear.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: List the risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Myopia (biggest), posterior vitreous detachment (key precipitant), increasing age (50s–70s), previous cataract surgery (pseudophakia), ocular trauma, previous retinal detachment (or in the other eye), family history, lattice degeneration, and diabetic retinopathy (tractional type).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the warning triad of retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Flashes (photopsia), floaters (a sudden increase/shower), and a 'curtain'/'shadow' descending across the visual field — all painless.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What are flashes (photopsia) in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Brief peripheral flashes of light caused by vitreous traction on the retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What do different floaters suggest in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: A sudden increase/shower of black spots or a 'cobweb'; a large single floater (Weiss ring) suggests PVD; a shower of tiny dots ('tobacco dust'/Shafer's sign) suggests a retinal tear.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the 'curtain' or 'shadow' in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: A progressive, painless shadow descending across the visual field — corresponding to the area of detached retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What happens to central vision in retinal detachment, and what sign appears in large detachments?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Central vision is preserved until the macula detaches; once the macula goes, central acuity drops and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) may appear in large detachments.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: How is posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) distinguished from retinal detachment clinically?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: PVD alone (very common, benign) also causes flashes and floaters — but a curtain/shadow or reduced vision suggests the PVD has caused a tear/detachment → refer. Any new flashes/floaters need assessment to exclude a break.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the significance of 'macula-ON' retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: The macula is still attached and central vision is intact → EXTREMELY urgent: operate before the macula detaches to preserve central vision (best outcomes, ideally within ~24 h). While waiting, posture the patient to keep fluid away from the macula.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the significance of 'macula-OFF' retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: The macula has already detached and central vision is lost → still urgent but the window is slightly less frantic (ideally within ~2–3 days); visual prognosis is already compromised as central vision often doesn't fully recover.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the key diagnostic test in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Dilated fundus examination (indirect ophthalmoscopy) — shows the detached retina (grey, elevated, mobile), identifies breaks/tears, and whether the macula is on or off.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is Shafer's sign?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Pigment cells/'tobacco dust' in the anterior vitreous on slit-lamp — suggestive of a retinal tear.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: When is B-scan ultrasound used in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: If the view is obscured (e.g. by vitreous haemorrhage or cataract).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the role of OCT in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: It assesses macular involvement (macula-on vs off), alongside visual acuity and RAPD assessment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the initial management of any suspected retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Refer for same-day ophthalmology assessment. While awaiting surgery, posture the patient to keep subretinal fluid away from the macula (position depends on the break location) and avoid strenuous activity.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: How is a retinal TEAR (before detachment) treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Laser retinopexy or cryotherapy — seals the break to prevent (further) detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What are the surgical options for established rhegmatogenous detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV — removes vitreous, drains subretinal fluid, seals breaks, + gas or silicone oil tamponade); scleral buckling (a silicone band indents the sclera to reappose the retina, favoured in younger/phakic eyes); and pneumatic retinopexy (an intraocular gas bubble tamponades a selected superior break, + laser/cryo). Anatomical success ~85–90%.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: How are tractional and exudative retinal detachments managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Treat the underlying cause — laser/vitrectomy for diabetic tractional detachment; BP control or treatment of tumour/inflammation for exudative detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the golden rule for new flashes and floaters?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Exclude a retinal tear — PVD alone is benign, but a curtain/shadow or reduced vision means refer.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Retinal damage from chronic (or acutely severe) high blood pressure — the eye's version of hypertensive target-organ damage.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: Why does hypertensive retinopathy matter clinically?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: The retina is the only place you can directly see the effects of hypertension on blood vessels; the grade correlates with cardiovascular/stroke risk and mortality; and its most severe form (grade 4/papilloedema) signals malignant (accelerated) hypertension — a medical emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are the three phases of hypertensive retinopathy pathophysiology?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: (1) Vasoconstrictive — arterioles constrict → generalised narrowing; (2) sclerotic — chronic pressure thickens the walls (arteriosclerosis) → copper/silver wiring + AV nipping; (3) exudative — the blood-retinal barrier breaks down → haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and (if severe) optic disc swelling.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is the key fork in hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Chronic (grades 1–3, sustained high BP, manage BP + cardiovascular risk) vs malignant hypertension (grade 4, severe BP often >180/120 with acute rise, papilloedema/macular star → emergency same-day assessment).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What grading system is used for hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: The Keith-Wagener-Barker classification (grades 1–4), where each grade builds on the previous.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 1 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Mild generalised arteriolar narrowing (vessels look thinner), ± increased tortuosity.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Grade 1 + focal arteriolar narrowing + AV nipping/nicking + copper wiring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Grade 2 + flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates + silver wiring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Grade 3 + papilloedema ± macular star = malignant hypertension.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is AV nipping (nicking)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: The vein appears pinched or deviated where a thickened, sclerotic artery crosses it — a sign of arteriosclerosis in hypertensive retinopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is the difference between copper wiring and silver wiring?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Increasingly sclerotic arterioles reflect light abnormally: copper wiring = moderate sclerosis; silver wiring = severe sclerosis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are cotton-wool spots and what do they represent?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Fluffy white patches that are nerve-fibre-layer microinfarcts (ischaemia).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are flame haemorrhages?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Superficial nerve-fibre-layer bleeds seen in hypertensive retinopathy (grade 3).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is a macular star?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Hard exudates (lipid/protein leakage) arranged in a star pattern around the fovea — seen in severe hypertensive retinopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What does papilloedema indicate in hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Optic disc swelling (grade 4) = malignant hypertension — a medical emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: Is hypertensive retinopathy usually symptomatic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Usually asymptomatic — found on routine fundoscopy. Malignant hypertension may cause headache, visual disturbance/blurring, and features of other end-organ damage (AKI, heart failure, encephalopathy).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What does sudden visual loss in a patient with hypertensive retinopathy suggest?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: A complication such as a retinal vein or artery occlusion (hypertension is a major risk factor).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What investigations are used in hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Blood pressure + fundoscopy/dilated fundus exam (grade the changes) drive the diagnosis. Assess other target-organ damage: urinalysis + U&Es (renal), ECG/echo (LVH); fundus photography/OCT/FFA for documentation. Screen for secondary hypertension if young/severe/resistant.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is the mainstay of treatment for hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Controlling the blood pressure — it is not primarily an 'eye' treatment. Most retinal changes stabilise or improve with good BP control.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: How is chronic (grades 1–3) hypertensive retinopathy managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Manage hypertension per standard guidelines (lifestyle + antihypertensives — ACE inhibitor/ARB, calcium-channel blocker, thiazide-like diuretic, per NICE) and address global cardiovascular risk (lipids, diabetes, smoking cessation).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: How is malignant hypertension (grade 4) managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Same-day specialist assessment/admission for severe hypertension (e.g. >180/120) with retinal haemorrhages/papilloedema or acute end-organ damage. Lower BP GRADUALLY — reduce by no more than ~25% in the first 24 hours (rapid reduction risks cerebral/retinal/renal ischaemia/infarction), using controllable agents (e.g. IV labetalol) with monitoring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: Why must blood pressure be lowered GRADUALLY in malignant hypertension?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Because rapid reduction risks cerebral, retinal and renal ischaemia/infarction — so reduce by no more than ~25% in the first 24 hours.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are the complications of hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Retinal vein or artery occlusion (hypertension is a major risk factor), macular oedema/exudative retinal detachment (severe cases), optic atrophy (prolonged papilloedema) → permanent visual loss, and worsening of co-existing diabetic retinopathy; it also marks elevated stroke/cardiac/renal risk.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: How do hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy signs differ on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Hypertension: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, copper/silver wiring. Diabetes: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, neovascularisation. (Cotton-wool spots occur in both.)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is herpes simplex keratitis and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Corneal infection/inflammation caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1) — the commonest infective cause of corneal blindness in the developed world. It is a sight-threatening cause of the painful red eye, it recurs, and topical steroids given for the epithelial form can dramatically worsen it and cause corneal perforation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the single most important teaching point about HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Topical corticosteroids given for the epithelial (dendritic) form dramatically worsen it and can cause corneal perforation — it is the classic reason NEVER to give steroid drops for an undiagnosed red eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the mechanism of HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: After primary infection, HSV-1 lies latent in the trigeminal ganglion. Triggers cause reactivation → the virus travels down the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) to the cornea → replicates in the epithelium → the characteristic branching dendritic ulcer. Repeated episodes drive stromal scarring and vision loss.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: Where does HSV-1 lie latent, and which nerve division does it travel down to reach the cornea?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Latent in the trigeminal ganglion; it reactivates and travels down the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the key fork in HSV keratitis, and what does it determine?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Epithelial (dendritic) vs stromal/disciform disease — this determines whether steroids are dangerous or necessary (the crux of management).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the nature and treatment of EPITHELIAL (dendritic) HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Active viral replication in the epithelium; the sign is a dendritic ulcer (branching, stains with fluorescein). Treatment is antiviral; topical steroids are CONTRAINDICATED.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the nature and treatment of STROMAL/disciform HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Immune-mediated stromal inflammation; signs include stromal haze/oedema, a disciform disc of oedema, neovascularisation and scarring. Treatment is antiviral PLUS topical steroid (under specialist supervision).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the 'golden rule' about steroids in epithelial HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: In epithelial (dendritic) disease, topical steroids promote viral replication → the dendrite enlarges into a geographic ('amoeboid') ulcer → risk of perforation. Steroids are only used in stromal/disciform (immune-driven) disease, always with antiviral cover under ophthalmology.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: List the risk factors/triggers for HSV keratitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Previous HSV eye disease (recurrence is the rule), UV/sunlight exposure, fever/systemic illness, physical/emotional stress, menstruation, immunosuppression (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy), atopic disease, topical/systemic corticosteroids, contact lens wear, and ocular surgery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What are the clinical features of HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: A painful, red, unilateral eye with foreign-body/gritty sensation, watering, photophobia; blurred vision if the central cornea/stroma is involved; reduced corneal sensation (a useful clue); and possibly vesicles on the eyelids/periocular skin.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: Why is reduced corneal sensation a useful clue in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Because HSV damages the corneal nerves, reducing corneal sensation — a helpful diagnostic pointer.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the pathognomonic sign of epithelial HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: A dendritic ulcer — a branching, serpentine epithelial ulcer with terminal bulbs that stains with fluorescein (green under blue light). Rose Bengal stains devitalised cells at the ulcer edges.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the key first investigation in suspected HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein — usually diagnostic (a dendrite confirms it) and assesses for stromal involvement.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What additional tests may be used in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Corneal sensation testing (reduced in HSV) and viral swab/PCR (corneal/conjunctival) if uncertain or atypical.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What must you NOT do before slit-lamp + fluorescein in any painful red eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Do NOT start steroid drops — fluorescein must first exclude a dendritic ulcer (steroids would risk a geographic ulcer/perforation).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the topical antiviral treatment for epithelial (dendritic) HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Topical antiviral — aciclovir 3% eye ointment (5×/day) or ganciclovir 0.15% gel (± trifluridine).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: When are oral antivirals used in HSV keratitis, and what other measures help epithelial disease?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Oral antiviral (aciclovir/valaciclovir) in some cases, and in the immunocompromised/severe/recurrent disease. Epithelial debridement (specialist) and a cycloplegic (cyclopentolate) for comfort also help. Do NOT use topical corticosteroids.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: How is stromal/disciform HSV keratitis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Topical corticosteroid PLUS antiviral cover, under ophthalmology supervision — because it is immune-mediated, steroids are needed, but always with antiviral cover.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What prophylaxis is used for recurrent HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Long-term oral aciclovir prophylaxis (reduces recurrence — the HEDS trial). Also UV protection (sunglasses).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the role of corneal transplant (keratoplasty) in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: For significant corneal scarring once the disease is quiescent.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What general/preventive measures apply in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Stop contact lenses, treat lid herpes, provide UV protection, and give prophylactic oral aciclovir for recurrent disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What are the complications of HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Recurrence (very common), corneal scarring → permanent visual loss (leading cause of corneal blindness), geographic/amoeboid ulcer (especially steroid-induced) → corneal melt/perforation, neurotrophic (metaherpetic) keratopathy (poor healing from nerve damage), secondary bacterial infection, and stromal neovascularisation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is neurotrophic (metaherpetic) keratopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Poor corneal healing resulting from HSV damage to the corneal nerves — a complication of recurrent HSV keratitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: How does HSV keratitis differ from herpes zoster ophthalmicus and Acanthamoeba keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: HSV: dendritic ulcer. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: vesicular rash in V1 + Hutchinson's sign (nose-tip involvement) → pseudodendrites. Acanthamoeba: contact-lens wearer with severe pain out of proportion to signs.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is diabetic retinopathy and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: A microvascular complication of diabetes in which chronic hyperglycaemia damages the retinal blood vessels → leakage, ischaemia and ultimately abnormal new-vessel growth. It is the leading cause of blindness in the working-age population (16–64) in the UK, largely preventable and detectable early by screening.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the core mechanism of diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Persistent hyperglycaemia damages the retinal capillary endothelium and pericytes → vessels become leaky (haemorrhages, exudates, oedema) and occluded (retinal ischaemia). Ischaemic retina releases VEGF → neovascularisation (fragile new vessels that bleed and scar).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: Why is every diabetic screened for retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Because it is asymptomatic until it threatens sight, but its sight-threatening stages (proliferative and maculopathy) are treatable if caught in time.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: Why are retinopathy (R) and maculopathy (M) graded on separate axes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Because maculopathy threatens central vision independently of the retinopathy stage.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the features of R1 (background/non-proliferative) retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Microaneurysms, dot/blot haemorrhages, and hard exudates.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the features of R2 (pre-proliferative) retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Cotton-wool spots (ischaemia), venous beading, IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities), and deeper haemorrhages.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What defines R3 (proliferative) retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: New vessels — at the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE) — the sight-threatening stage requiring urgent referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What defines M1 (maculopathy)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Exudates/haemorrhage/oedema within ~1 disc diameter of the fovea — the commonest cause of visual loss in diabetes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the exam shortcut for grading diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Microaneurysms + hard exudates → background (R1); cotton-wool spots + venous beading + IRMA → pre-proliferative (R2); new vessels → proliferative (R3, urgent referral); changes near the fovea → maculopathy (M1).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the types of diabetic maculopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Focal/diffuse exudative (leakage); ischaemic (macular capillary non-perfusion — poorer prognosis); and clinically significant macular oedema (CSMO — the treatment threshold).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the biggest risk factor for diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Duration of diabetes — most type 1 diabetics have some retinopathy after ~20 years.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: List the risk factors for diabetic retinopathy.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Duration of diabetes (biggest), poor glycaemic control (high HbA1c), hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, pregnancy (can accelerate — needs extra screening), renal disease, and smoking.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is an important warning about rapidly tightening glucose control?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: It can cause transient early worsening of retinopathy — warn patients.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the clinical features of diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Asymptomatic in early stages (hence screening); gradual reduction in visual acuity (especially maculopathy affecting central/reading vision); floaters or sudden visual loss suggesting vitreous haemorrhage (from proliferative new vessels); and distortion from maculopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the UK Diabetic Eye Screening Programme?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Annual digital retinal photography through dilated pupils for all diabetics from age 12.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for macular oedema in diabetes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: OCT — it quantifies retinal thickening to detect and monitor macular oedema.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the role of fundus fluorescein angiography in diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: It maps ischaemia and neovascularisation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the referral timelines for diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: R3 (proliferative) → urgent (~2 weeks); M1 (maculopathy) or R2 (pre-proliferative) → routine ophthalmology referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What systemic management applies to all diabetic retinopathy patients?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Optimise glycaemic control (individualised HbA1c, e.g. ~48–53 mmol/mol), blood pressure control (<140/80, tighter if renal disease), lipid management (statin), smoking cessation, and extra screening in pregnancy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the first-line treatment for proliferative (R3) diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) — laser burns to the peripheral ischaemic retina ablate VEGF-producing tissue so new vessels regress.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the side effects of pan-retinal photocoagulation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Peripheral field loss and reduced night vision/contrast — it sacrifices peripheral retina to save central vision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the second-line/adjunct treatments for proliferative retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Anti-VEGF (second-line if active despite complete PRP); vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the first-line treatment for centre-involving diabetic macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, faricimab).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the treatment for non-centre-involving diabetic macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Macular laser (the default). Intravitreal steroids (dexamethasone implant) are an option, with cataract/IOP risk.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the complications of diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Vitreous haemorrhage (sudden visual loss/floaters), tractional retinal detachment (fibrous scaffolding contracts), neovascular glaucoma (iris/angle neovascularisation — 'rubeosis iridis'), and permanent visual loss/blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is rubeosis iridis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Neovascularisation of the iris/angle in advanced diabetic retinopathy, which causes neovascular glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: How do diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy signs differ on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Diabetes: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, neovascularisation. Hypertension: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, copper/silver wiring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is chronic open-angle glaucoma (COAG/POAG)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: A progressive optic neuropathy — characteristic optic-nerve-head damage with corresponding visual field loss — usually (not always) associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP). It is the commonest glaucoma and a leading cause of irreversible blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Why is COAG described as a disease 'found by screening'?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Because it is asymptomatic until advanced — painless, gradual peripheral field loss the patient doesn't notice until central vision is threatened — so early detection (optometrist/screening) plus IOP-lowering prevents blindness, but damage already done is permanent.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the core mechanism of COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: There is increased resistance to aqueous outflow through an anatomically OPEN angle → IOP rises (or the nerve is susceptible even at 'normal' pressure) → pressure damages retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic nerve head → disc cupping + arcuate/peripheral field defects.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: How does COAG differ from acute angle-closure glaucoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: COAG: open angle, chronic/insidious, painless, white eye, gradual PERIPHERAL field loss, mildly-moderately raised IOP, detected on screening. AACG: closed angle, sudden emergency, severe pain, red eye, sudden loss with haloes, very high IOP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What are the risk factors for COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Increasing age (dominant), raised IOP (major modifiable risk), family history (first-degree relative — strong), Black/African-Caribbean ethnicity (earlier, more aggressive), myopia, diabetes, hypertension, and corticosteroid use (steroid-responders).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Which ethnicity is at higher risk of COAG (and how does this contrast with angle-closure)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Black/African-Caribbean people develop COAG earlier and more aggressively; by contrast, angle-closure glaucoma is commoner in East Asians.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the major MODIFIABLE risk factor for COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Raised intraocular pressure.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Why is COAG asymptomatic in early disease?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Because it causes gradual, painless loss of PERIPHERAL vision that patients don't notice, with central vision preserved until late — so it is often detected only on a routine optician visit.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the characteristic pattern of visual loss in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Gradual, painless loss of PERIPHERAL vision progressing to 'tunnel vision' in advanced disease, with central vision preserved until late (the opposite of AMD).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the diagnostic triad of COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: (1) Raised IOP (though normal-tension glaucoma exists); (2) optic disc cupping (increased cup-to-disc ratio); (3) visual field defects.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What optic disc changes are seen in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Increased cup-to-disc ratio (>0.5, or asymmetry), neuroretinal rim thinning, vessel 'bayoneting', notching, and disc haemorrhages.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What visual field defects occur in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Arcuate scotomas and a nasal step, progressing to peripheral constriction (tunnel vision).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is normal-tension glaucoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Typical glaucomatous optic nerve damage and field loss occurring at a 'normal' IOP — a recognised variant of COAG where the nerve is susceptible even at normal pressures.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the standard test to measure IOP in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Goldmann applanation tonometry.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the role of gonioscopy in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: It confirms the angle is OPEN, distinguishing COAG from angle-closure glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What investigations are used in COAG (NICE NG81)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Goldmann applanation tonometry (IOP), gonioscopy (open angle), visual field testing/perimetry (maps and monitors field loss), optic nerve assessment (fundoscopy/OCT of disc and retinal nerve fibre layer), and central corneal thickness (pachymetry).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Why is central corneal thickness (pachymetry) measured in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: A thin cornea underestimates the true IOP and is also an independent risk factor for glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the aim of COAG treatment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: To lower IOP to slow/halt progression and preserve remaining vision — damage already done is irreversible.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the first-line treatment for newly diagnosed COAG (NICE 2022)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: 360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) — a major 2022 change (based on the LiGHT trial). Laser to the trabecular meshwork improves outflow and can delay or avoid eye drops. Also offered for ocular hypertension with IOP ≥24 mmHg.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the first-line DRUG (drop) for COAG and its mechanism?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: A prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) — increases uveoscleral outflow; once-daily. Used if SLT is declined/unsuitable, or as an add-on.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What are the side effects of latanoprost (prostaglandin analogue)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Iris/periocular pigmentation, eyelash growth, and conjunctival hyperaemia.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What are the other classes of IOP-lowering drops in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Beta-blocker (timolol — reduces production, caution in asthma/COPD/bradycardia); carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (dorzolamide; oral acetazolamide — reduces production); alpha-2 agonist (brimonidine — reduces production + increases outflow); and miotics (pilocarpine — increases outflow, less used).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What surgical options exist for COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Trabeculectomy (creates a new drainage channel — a guarded fistula to a subconjunctival 'bleb') for advanced/uncontrolled disease; and MIGS (minimally invasive glaucoma surgery)/drainage tubes/shunts, increasingly used.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What monitoring and general measures apply in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Lifelong follow-up (IOP, visual fields, disc/OCT), screening first-degree relatives, and reporting significant field loss to the DVLA (driving).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the key prognostic point about vision loss in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Vision loss is IRREVERSIBLE — treatment prevents further loss but cannot restore what is lost. Hence lifelong monitoring and screening of relatives.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: How does COAG contrast with AMD in the pattern of vision loss?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: COAG causes peripheral (tunnel) loss with central vision preserved until late; AMD causes central vision loss with preserved peripheral vision — opposite patterns.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Thrombotic occlusion of the central retinal vein → blockage of venous drainage → back-pressure causing widespread retinal haemorrhage, oedema and (if severe) ischaemia. It is a common cause of sudden painless visual loss in older adults and is the venous counterpart to CRAO.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How does the core mechanism of CRVO contrast with CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: CRAO is arterial (no blood IN → pale retina). CRVO is venous (blood can't get OUT → back-pressure → the retina engorges, haemorrhages and swells).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why does CRVO share arterial risk factors despite being a venous event?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: The thrombus forms where the central retinal vein shares a sheath with the stiff atherosclerotic central retinal artery at the lamina cribrosa — so hypertension and atherosclerosis are risk factors.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the two types of CRVO and their relative frequency?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Non-ischaemic (~75%) — milder, better vision (often >6/60), absent/mild RAPD, <10 disc areas of non-perfusion; and ischaemic (~25%) — severe, poor vision (often <6/60), marked RAPD, >10 disc areas of non-perfusion.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why does the ischaemic-vs-non-ischaemic distinction matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: The ischaemic type drives VEGF release → neovascularisation of the iris/angle → neovascular glaucoma ('90-day glaucoma') + vitreous haemorrhage. Non-ischaemic CRVO can also convert to ischaemic, so all need monitoring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Roughly what proportion of non-ischaemic CRVO converts to ischaemic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: About one-third.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the commonest risk factor for CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Hypertension (with atherosclerosis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: List the risk factors for CRVO.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Increasing age (>50), hypertension (commonest), hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, smoking, raised intraocular pressure/glaucoma (a specific CRVO risk), hyperviscosity/thrombophilia (polycythaemia, myeloma, antiphospholipid syndrome), inflammatory/vasculitic causes (Behçet's, sarcoidosis), and the oral contraceptive pill (younger patients).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Which CRVO risk factor is specific to the eye rather than systemic vasculature?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Raised intraocular pressure/glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: When should hyperviscosity/thrombophilia causes be considered in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: In younger patients, or bilateral/recurrent cases — consider polycythaemia, myeloma, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C/S deficiency and autoimmune/inflammatory causes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the typical presentation of CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Sudden, painless loss/blurring of vision in ONE eye, of variable severity (mild blurring to profound loss), often noticed on waking (venous stasis overnight).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What pupillary sign indicates ischaemic CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A marked relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — a marker of severity.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the classic fundoscopic picture of CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A 'blood and thunder' fundus — widespread flame and blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants (hallmark); dilated, tortuous veins; cotton-wool spots; optic disc swelling; and macular oedema.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How does branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) differ from CRVO on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: BRVO: haemorrhages confined to one sector/quadrant drained by the blocked branch, classically at an arteriovenous crossing. CRVO: haemorrhages in all four quadrants.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How is CRVO diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Largely clinically on fundoscopy/slit-lamp, supported by OCT (quantifies macular oedema) and fundus fluorescein angiography (assesses capillary non-perfusion to classify ischaemic vs non-ischaemic, best once haemorrhage clears).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the role of OCT in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: It quantifies macular oedema — key for guiding and monitoring treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the role of fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: It assesses capillary non-perfusion to classify ischaemic vs non-ischaemic CRVO (best done once the haemorrhage clears).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What systemic work-up is done in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: BP, fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipids, FBC (polycythaemia/hyperviscosity), ESR, and intraocular pressure. In young/bilateral/recurrent cases, add a thrombophilia and inflammatory screen (antiphospholipid, protein C/S, myeloma, autoimmune).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the first-line/gold-standard treatment for CRVO macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab, faricimab) — they improve vision and reduce oedema; early treatment gives better outcomes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the second-line/adjunct treatment for CRVO macular oedema, and its risks?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Intravitreal steroids (dexamethasone implant/triamcinolone) — with the risks of cataract and raised IOP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Is macular grid laser recommended for CRVO macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: No — unlike in BRVO, macular grid laser is NOT recommended for CRVO macular oedema (it reduces leakage on angiography but gives no visual benefit — CVOS).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How is neovascularisation / ischaemic CRVO treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) — laser to ablate ischaemic retina, reducing the VEGF drive, for neovascularisation of the iris/angle/retina (prevents/treats neovascular glaucoma); anti-VEGF is a useful adjunct.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How closely should ischaemic CRVO be monitored, and why?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Review approximately 1–2 monthly in the first year to detect neovascularisation early (which drives neovascular glaucoma and vitreous haemorrhage).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What systemic management is important in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Treat cardiovascular risk factors — control BP, lipids, diabetes; smoking cessation — to reduce risk to the fellow eye, and address any hyperviscosity/thrombophilia/inflammatory cause. CRVO is a marker of systemic vascular disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the complications of CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Macular oedema (commonest cause of visual loss), neovascular glaucoma (from iris/angle neovascularisation in the ischaemic type — painful, sight-threatening, '90-day glaucoma'), vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, and macular ischaemia (permanent central loss).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is 'neovascular glaucoma' / '90-day glaucoma' in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Neovascular glaucoma from iris/angle neovascularisation driven by ischaemia, classically developing around 90 days after ischaemic CRVO — a painful, sight-threatening complication.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Sudden occlusion of the central retinal artery → acute ischaemia of the inner retina → sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in one eye. It is a 'stroke of the eye' and a warning of imminent stroke and cardiovascular events.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why has the modern emphasis in CRAO shifted, given vision is often lost permanently?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Towards treating the patient as a stroke (urgent work-up + secondary prevention) and not missing giant cell arteritis (treatable → saves the other eye).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What part of the retina does the central retinal artery supply, and what is its origin?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: It supplies the INNER retina. It is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, which is the first branch of the internal carotid artery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why does the fovea show a 'cherry-red spot' in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: The inner retina infarcts and becomes pale/oedematous, but the fovea is thin and shows the underlying choroidal circulation through it, appearing as a cherry-red spot against the pale retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the two types of CRAO and their relative frequency?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Non-arteritic (~>95%) — embolus/thrombosis (carotid atheroma, cardiac); and arteritic (<5%) — giant cell arteritis (± other vasculitides).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What clues suggest ARTERITIC CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Age >50 with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms, and raised ESR/CRP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the action for arteritic CRAO and why is it urgent?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Immediate high-dose corticosteroids (don't wait for biopsy) — to protect/save the fellow eye, as missing it risks rapid, bilateral, irreversible blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What must always be asked/checked in any patient over 50 with CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Ask about GCA symptoms (headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR) and check ESR/CRP — missing arteritic CRAO risks rapid bilateral blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the commonest embolic source in non-arteritic CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Carotid artery atherosclerosis (calcific/cholesterol emboli).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What cardiac sources can cause CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: AF, valvular disease, endocarditis, and post-MI mural thrombus.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: List the vascular risk factors for non-arteritic CRAO.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, smoking, hypercoagulable states, vasculitis, and sickle cell disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the classic presentation of CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Sudden, painless, severe loss of vision in ONE eye — often 'counting fingers' or worse, and may be complete.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What may precede CRAO and what does it suggest?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Amaurosis fugax — transient 'curtain' visual loss — which suggests a carotid embolic source.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What pupillary sign is found in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — the affected pupil dilates on the swinging-light test.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the fundoscopy findings in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A pale, oedematous ('whitened') retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea (classic); attenuated (thread-like) arteries; segmentation of the blood column ('cattle-trucking'); and sometimes a visible embolus (Hollenhorst plaque) at a bifurcation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is a Hollenhorst plaque?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A visible cholesterol embolus seen at a retinal arterial bifurcation, indicating a carotid embolic source.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What urgent blood tests are done in CRAO and why?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Urgent ESR and CRP (± temporal artery biopsy) to exclude giant cell arteritis — immediately in those over 50.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What further investigations form the 'stroke-like' work-up of CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: FBC, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, clotting; ECG (AF) and carotid Doppler ultrasound (carotid stenosis); echocardiogram if a cardiac source is suspected; OCT (retinal oedema) and fundus fluorescein angiography (delayed arterial filling) to confirm; brain imaging as part of the stroke pathway; and BP/vascular risk assessment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the first management priority in a patient over 50 with CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Exclude/treat GCA — if arteritic (GCA) is suspected, give immediate high-dose corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone / high-dose oral prednisolone) before biopsy to protect the fellow eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What acute 'eye' measures may be attempted in CRAO (and their evidence level)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Ocular massage (intermittent digital globe pressure to dislodge an embolus), lowering IOP (IV acetazolamide ± mannitol, anterior chamber paracentesis), inhaled carbogen/rebreathing (CO2 → retinal vasodilation), and sublingual GTN — all low-evidence.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the evolving role of thrombolysis in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: IV thrombolysis (tPA/alteplase) within a narrow early window (~<4.5 hours) is increasingly considered at stroke centres, with recent meta-analyses suggesting benefit with early treatment — but it is not universally established. Manage within a stroke-pathway framework, where transfer takes priority over ocular massage.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the most important long-term step in CRAO management?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Secondary prevention — treat as a TIA/stroke: antiplatelet therapy, manage carotid stenosis (endarterectomy if significant), anticoagulate AF, control BP/lipids/diabetes, and smoking cessation. This prevents the next cerebral stroke or MI — the real threat to the patient.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the ocular complications of CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Permanent visual loss (usual outcome — ~80% counting-fingers or worse), and ocular neovascularisation (retinal ischaemia drives VEGF) → neovascular glaucoma and vitreous haemorrhage → follow up ~monthly for up to ~4 months.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the systemic danger after CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Subsequent stroke or MI — the real threat to the patient, which is why secondary prevention is the priority.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How does CRAO differ from central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: CRAO: pale oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot. CRVO: the venous counterpart — a 'blood and thunder' fundus (widespread haemorrhages), not a pale retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the differential for a cherry-red spot besides CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs in infants (CRAO is in the elderly and acute).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a cataract and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: An opacification (clouding) of the normally transparent crystalline lens. It is the leading cause of blindness worldwide and the commonest treatable cause of visual impairment; cataract surgery is the most frequently performed NHS operation and one of the most successful in medicine.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the core mechanism of cataract formation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: The lens is normally kept clear by orderly proteins (crystallins). With ageing and oxidative stress (or metabolic/toxic insults), these proteins denature and aggregate, scattering light → the lens clouds → light can't focus cleanly on the retina → blurred vision, glare and dimmed colours.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the commonest type/cause of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Age-related (senile) cataract — from ageing and oxidative stress.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What are the secondary causes of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Diabetes, corticosteroids, trauma, uveitis, radiation, high myopia, and previous eye surgery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What causes congenital cataract, and how is it detected?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Detected early by an absent red reflex (newborn/6-week check). Causes include intrauterine infection (rubella), galactosaemia, Down syndrome, and hereditary causes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a nuclear sclerotic cataract and its characteristic effect?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: The commonest age-related type, affecting the central lens; it causes a myopic shift ('second sight' — some elderly people transiently read without glasses).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a cortical cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Spoke-like wedge opacities from the lens periphery; prominent glare.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a posterior subcapsular cataract and its associations?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Opacity at the back of the lens, associated with steroids and diabetes; causes disproportionate glare and near-vision difficulty and progresses faster.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the dominant risk factor for cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Increasing age.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: List the risk factors for cataract.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Increasing age (dominant), smoking and high alcohol intake, diabetes mellitus/metabolic disorders, corticosteroids (systemic or topical — the classic drug cause), UV/sunlight, ionising radiation, ocular trauma, previous intraocular surgery, uveitis, high myopia, and congenital/hereditary causes/intrauterine infection.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: Which drug class is the classic drug cause of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Corticosteroids (systemic or topical) — associated with posterior subcapsular cataract.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What are the typical clinical features of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Gradual, painless loss/blurring of vision over months–years; glare (bright lights, night headlights, haloes); faded/yellowed colours; reduced contrast sensitivity; occasionally monocular diplopia; myopic shift (nuclear); usually bilateral but asymmetric.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the key examination sign of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Loss of the red reflex (or a dark opacity silhouetted against it). The lens may look cloudy/grey when advanced.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What does an absent red reflex in a neonate indicate, and what must be done?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: A congenital cataract → URGENT referral (part of the newborn/6-week check).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: How is cataract diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Clinically — visual acuity + slit-lamp examination (grades and localises the cataract) + red reflex/ophthalmoscopy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What pre-operative assessment is needed before cataract surgery?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Biometry (measures the eye to calculate the intraocular lens power) and assessment for co-existing eye disease (glaucoma, AMD, diabetic retinopathy) that would limit visual benefit.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What investigations are needed for a congenital cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Investigate the cause — TORCH screen, galactosaemia testing, and a metabolic/genetic work-up.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: Is there any medical treatment that reverses or halts cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: No — surgery is the only cure. Interim measures (stronger glasses, brighter reading lights) may help mild cataract, plus modifying risk factors (stop smoking, glycaemic control).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the definitive surgical treatment for cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Phacoemulsification — ultrasound emulsifies and aspirates the cloudy lens through a small incision, and an artificial intraocular lens (IOL) is implanted. Usually a day-case under local anaesthetic.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is given during cataract surgery to prevent endophthalmitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Intracameral cefuroxime.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What are the NICE (NG77) referral criteria for cataract surgery?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Do NOT restrict access on visual acuity alone. Offer surgery when the cataract affects quality of life (after discussing risks/benefits) — a functional decision, not a fixed acuity cut-off. Second-eye surgery uses the same criteria.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is endophthalmitis and how does it present after cataract surgery?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: A rare but serious intraocular infection — a painful red eye with visual loss days after surgery. It is a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is posterior capsule opacification (PCO) and how is it treated?
