conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: The commonest late complication ('secondary cataract'): the capsule behind the IOL clouds months–years after surgery. Treated with YAG laser capsulotomy (quick and effective).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: List the complications of cataract surgery.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Endophthalmitis (emergency), posterior capsule opacification (commonest late → YAG laser), posterior capsule rupture (intraoperative), retinal detachment, cystoid macular oedema, IOL dislocation, and raised IOP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is bacterial conjunctivitis and where does it sit among red-eye causes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: A bacterial infection of the conjunctiva — one of the three common causes of the 'red eye' (with viral and allergic). It is very common and mostly benign/self-limiting, but a few presentations are sight- or life-threatening.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is the core clinical skill in acute infective conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Recognising that most cases are a self-limiting nuisance, and spotting the minority that is sight- or life-threatening (gonococcal, chlamydial, neonatal, contact-lens-related) — while reassuring the rest.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How does the discharge differ between bacterial, viral and allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Bacterial: purulent, sticky (yellow-green), lids stuck together on waking. Viral: watery. Allergic: watery/stringy with prominent itch.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How does laterality differ between bacterial, viral and allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Bacterial: often starts unilateral then spreads. Viral: often bilateral (one then the other). Allergic: bilateral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What red-flag-free features do all three common conjunctivitides share?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Red eye, normal vision, no significant pain, no photophobia, normal pupil. If any of these red flags are present → think keratitis, uveitis, scleritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma instead.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the common causative organisms of bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (especially in children), and Moraxella.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: Which organism causes contact-lens-related bacterial conjunctivitis/keratitis, and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Gram-negative) — high risk of keratitis/corneal ulcer; Acanthamoeba is another contact-lens-associated cause. These threaten sight.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the features of gonococcal conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Hyperacute onset with copious purulent discharge, rapidly sight-threatening (corneal perforation) — caused by N. gonorrhoeae.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the features of chlamydial conjunctivitis, and its global significance?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Chronic/subacute conjunctivitis caused by C. trachomatis; trachoma (serotypes A–C) is the world's leading infective cause of blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the classic clinical features of bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: A red, gritty, 'sore' eye (foreign-body sensation, not true pain) with purulent/mucopurulent discharge; eyelids crusted/stuck together in the morning; discharge re-accumulates within minutes of wiping. Usually starts in one eye and spreads; vision normal, no significant pain/photophobia, pupil normal; diffuse conjunctival injection toward the fornices.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How is bacterial conjunctivitis usually diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Clinically — history and examination; no tests for routine cases.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: When are swabs (MC&S + chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT) indicated in conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: For severe/hyperacute cases, suspected gonococcal/chlamydial infection, neonatal conjunctivitis, contact-lens wearers, the immunocompromised, or treatment failure.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: When is fluorescein staining used in suspected conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: If corneal involvement is suspected — to rule out an ulcer/keratitis, especially in contact-lens wearers.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is the first-line management of routine bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Supportive care: reassurance (most resolve within 5–7 days without treatment), bathing/cleaning lids with cotton wool and cooled boiled water/saline to remove crusts, and hygiene measures. Antibiotics are often unnecessary.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What hygiene advice is given in bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Hand-washing, don't share towels/pillows (it is contagious), avoid eye-rubbing and contact lenses until resolved. School/work exclusion is not routinely required (UKHSA).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is the first-line topical antibiotic for bacterial conjunctivitis, and how can it be prescribed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Chloramphenicol (0.5% drops / 1% ointment) — broad-spectrum, available OTC. A delayed prescription (start if not improving after ~3 days) is reasonable.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is the alternative topical antibiotic to chloramphenicol, and when is it useful?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Fusidic acid — an alternative (no Gram-negative cover), useful in pregnancy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the cautions with chloramphenicol?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Avoid in prior myelosuppression/blood dyscrasia; avoid in pregnancy (use fusidic acid instead).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How should a contact-lens wearer with a red eye be managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Stop lens wear and have a low threshold to refer — to exclude microbial keratitis (Pseudomonas/Acanthamoeba), which is sight-threatening.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How is gonococcal conjunctivitis treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Systemic ceftriaxone plus urgent ophthalmology referral (it is hyperacute and sight-threatening).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How is chlamydial conjunctivitis treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Systemic azithromycin or doxycycline plus GUM referral/contact tracing (it is an STI).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is ophthalmia neonatorum and how is it managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Neonatal conjunctivitis in the first 28 days — gonococcal (within 48 h, sight-threatening) or chlamydial (5–14 days), acquired from the maternal genital tract. It must ALWAYS be referred urgently.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How does bacterial conjunctivitis differ from viral conjunctivitis on associated features?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Viral is watery with a preauricular lymph node, follicles, and a recent URTI; bacterial has purulent sticky discharge and lacks these viral associations.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is allergic conjunctivitis and what hypersensitivity mechanism underlies it?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity inflammation of the conjunctiva in response to an allergen. It is extremely common, often alongside allergic rhinitis ('hay fever eyes').

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: Describe the mechanism of allergic conjunctivitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Allergen contacts the conjunctiva → binds IgE on mast cells → degranulation → histamine release → itch, redness, watering and swelling. This is why antihistamines (block the effect) and mast-cell stabilisers (prevent the release) are the treatments.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is the hallmark symptom of allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Itch — prominent and the most specific symptom; the eye is typically bilateral, watery and red.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What features are NOT part of allergic conjunctivitis and should prompt exclusion of a dangerous red eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Significant pain, marked photophobia, reduced vision, or an abnormal pupil — their presence means you must exclude keratitis, anterior uveitis, scleritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How does the discharge and laterality of allergic conjunctivitis compare with bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Allergic: bilateral, watery/stringy mucoid discharge, prominent itch. Bacterial: often unilateral (or spreads), purulent discharge, less itch.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is seasonal allergic conjunctivitis (SAC)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: The commonest type — caused by pollen (grass, tree), occurring in spring/summer ('hay fever'), often with allergic rhinitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is perennial allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A year-round form caused by house dust mite, animal dander or mould.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A more severe, chronic form in children/young males, with large 'cobblestone' giant papillae under the upper lid; it can threaten sight (corneal involvement) and needs specialist care.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is atopic keratoconjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A chronic, sight-threatening form in adults with atopic dermatitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is giant papillary conjunctivitis associated with?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Contact lenses, sutures or ocular prostheses.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is chemosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Conjunctival oedema — a swollen, 'boggy', sometimes gelatinous conjunctiva — a characteristic sign of allergic conjunctivitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What are the typical clinical features of allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Bilateral itching (dominant), watery/stringy mucoid discharge, red injected conjunctiva, chemosis, eyelid swelling, tearing, and often associated rhinitis and personal/family atopy (asthma, eczema, hay fever). Papillae ('cobblestones') may be seen on lid eversion, especially in VKC.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How is allergic conjunctivitis diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Clinically — history (itch, bilateral, atopy, seasonality) and examination are usually sufficient. No routine tests are needed.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When might allergy testing (skin-prick/RAST) be considered in allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: If the trigger is unclear or symptoms are severe/persistent.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When should allergic conjunctivitis be referred?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: If the diagnosis is uncertain, red flags are present, or a severe/sight-threatening form (VKC/atopic keratoconjunctivitis) is suspected.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What are the first, non-pharmacological management steps for allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Allergen avoidance (the foundation), cool compresses, artificial tears/lubricants (to dilute and wash out allergen and soothe), avoiding eye rubbing, and avoiding contact lenses during flares.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is the first-line topical drug treatment for allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Topical antihistamines (azelastine, olopatadine, ketotifen — many are dual-action antihistamine + mast-cell stabiliser) — giving rapid relief, good for acute/intermittent symptoms.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How do topical mast-cell stabilisers work and what is their key limitation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Sodium cromoglicate, nedocromil, lodoxamide prevent mast-cell degranulation (prophylactic) but do NOT relieve established symptoms and take days–weeks to work — so start them BEFORE the season.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is the key distinction between antihistamines and mast-cell stabilisers in allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Antihistamines RELIEVE established symptoms rapidly; mast-cell stabilisers PREVENT symptoms but don't relieve them and are slow-onset — so they must be started early.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When are oral antihistamines used in allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: When there is associated allergic rhinitis or systemic allergy (cetirizine, loratadine).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When are topical corticosteroids used in allergic conjunctivitis, and what are the risks?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Only for severe/resistant disease and under specialist/ophthalmology supervision — because of the risks of raised IOP/glaucoma, cataract, and worsening herpetic keratitis. Never prescribe steroid drops for a red eye without excluding these.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How are vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: With specialist care — topical steroids and ciclosporin — because they are chronic and sight-threatening.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Progressive degeneration of the macula — the central retina responsible for high-acuity central vision — and the leading cause of irreversible visual loss in older adults in the developed world.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What vision does AMD affect and what does it spare?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: It robs CENTRAL vision (reading, driving, recognising faces) while sparing PERIPHERAL vision — so patients are rarely completely blind.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What structures does AMD damage at the macula?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), Bruch's membrane and photoreceptors at the macula.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What are drusen and their significance?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Yellow deposits of metabolic waste that accumulate at the macula — the hallmark of AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the frequency and mechanism of DRY (atrophic) AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: ~85–90% of cases. Gradual RPE/photoreceptor atrophy with drusen; late disease is geographic atrophy. Driven by oxidative stress and ageing.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the frequency and mechanism of WET (neovascular) AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: ~10–15% of cases. Choroidal neovascularisation — abnormal vessels grow from the choroid through Bruch's membrane and leak/bleed. Driven by VEGF.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: How does the onset differ between dry and wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Dry: gradual over years, slow progressive loss. Wet: rapid (days–weeks) with sudden central loss/distortion — responsible for ~90% of severe visual loss in AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the key clinical instinct for wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: An elderly patient with SUDDEN central visual distortion → suspect wet AMD → urgent referral (there is a treatable window). Gradual bilateral central blurring over years suggests dry AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the biggest MODIFIABLE risk factor for AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Smoking — strongly linked and the biggest modifiable risk.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: List the risk factors for AMD.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Increasing age (dominant), smoking (biggest modifiable), family history/genetics (complement factor H polymorphisms), Caucasian ethnicity, hypertension/cardiovascular disease, poor diet (low antioxidants), and female sex.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is metamorphopsia and how is it tested?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Straight lines appearing wavy/distorted — a classic symptom (especially wet AMD), tested with an Amsler grid.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is a central scotoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: A blank/dark central patch in the visual field — a feature of AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What visual symptoms occur in AMD besides distortion and scotoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Reduced acuity, difficulty reading/recognising faces, poor low-light adaptation, and micropsia/macropsia (objects appearing smaller/larger).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: Why is preserved peripheral vision important in AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: It provides reassurance (patients are not totally blind) and distinguishes AMD from glaucoma (which causes peripheral loss).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What are the fundoscopy findings in dry AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Drusen (yellow macular deposits), RPE pigmentary changes, and geographic atrophy in advanced disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What are the fundoscopy findings in wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Macular haemorrhage, exudates, fluid/oedema, and sometimes a grey-green subretinal (neovascular) membrane.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the KEY investigation in AMD and what does it show?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) — cross-sectional retinal imaging showing fluid (intra-/subretinal), drusen and neovascular membranes; it guides diagnosis and monitors treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the role of fluorescein angiography (FFA) in AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: It confirms and localises choroidal neovascularisation in wet AMD (showing leakage).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the role of the Amsler grid?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: A bedside test (and self-monitoring tool) where the patient reports distorted or missing lines — useful for detecting metamorphopsia and conversion of dry to wet AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: How is DRY AMD managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: No cure to reverse it → supportive measures and slowing progression: smoking cessation, AREDS2 supplements, low-vision aids, sight-impaired registration, and Amsler grid self-monitoring to catch conversion to wet AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What are AREDS2 supplements and what do they do?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: High-dose antioxidants — vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein and zeaxanthin — that slow progression from intermediate to advanced AMD (they do NOT reverse it or help early AMD).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What new treatments slow geographic atrophy in dry AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Complement inhibitors — pegcetacoplan (C3) and avacincaptad (C5), given intravitreally (FDA-approved 2023). They slow the lesion but do NOT improve vision; NICE approval is evolving.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the mainstay, sight-saving treatment for WET AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections — ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab (and newer faricimab, brolucizumab) — which block VEGF to halt neovascularisation and leakage. A loading course then maintenance ('treat-and-extend'/PRN, guided by OCT).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: Why is referral urgent in suspected wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Because early anti-VEGF treatment preserves vision (a treatable window), so urgent referral to a rapid-access macular clinic is needed.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: How does AMD differ from glaucoma in the pattern of vision loss?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: AMD causes central vision loss with preserved peripheral vision; glaucoma causes peripheral (tunnel) loss with central vision preserved until late — opposite patterns.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: A sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency in which the drainage angle of the anterior chamber becomes suddenly blocked, causing intraocular pressure (IOP) to rise rapidly and severely (often 50–80 mmHg vs normal 10–21). Delayed treatment causes irreversible optic nerve damage and permanent blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the normal range of intraocular pressure, and what is it in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Normal 10–21 mmHg; in AACG it is often 50–80 mmHg (usually >40–50).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Describe the normal flow of aqueous humour.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Aqueous is made by the ciliary body → flows from the posterior chamber → through the pupil → into the anterior chamber → drains via the trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the mechanism of pupillary block in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: In a susceptible eye (shallow anterior chamber, narrow angle), the iris bows forward and blocks the pupil ('pupillary block') → aqueous can't pass forward → pressure balloons the iris forward → it seals off the drainage angle → IOP shoots up.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What pupil state most commonly triggers AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Pupil dilation — mid-dilation is worst, as the iris bunches into the angle.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the classic clinical triad of AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Red painful eye + reduced vision/haloes around lights + nausea and vomiting.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What are the classic pupil and corneal signs of AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: A fixed, mid-dilated, oval, non-reactive pupil, and a hazy/cloudy (oedematous) cornea with reduced red reflex. There is also ciliary injection and a shallow anterior chamber, and the eye may feel hard ('like a marble') on palpation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Which refractive error is the classic risk factor for AACG and why?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) — small eyes with shallow anterior chambers and narrow angles.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: List the risk factors for AACG.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Hypermetropia (classic), increasing age (lens thickens/moves forward), female sex, Asian ethnicity, family history, and mydriasis-provoking triggers.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What triggers can provoke AACG via mydriasis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Dim light (cinema/dark room), pupil-dilating drugs (anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics, some antihistamines), and pharmacological dilation for fundoscopy (a classic exam trigger).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Why can AACG masquerade as an acute abdomen or migraine?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Because vagally-mediated nausea and vomiting may dominate the presentation and mislead, alongside headache — the eye signs can be overlooked.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the key confirmatory investigation in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Tonometry — measuring IOP (often >40–50 mmHg).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the role of gonioscopy in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: It visualises the closed drainage angle — the definitive angle assessment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Why must the fellow (other) eye be assessed in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Because it is usually also narrow-angled and predisposed → it needs prophylactic treatment (laser peripheral iridotomy).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What are the immediate general measures in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Immediate ophthalmology referral; start IOP-lowering treatment while awaiting them; lie the patient flat, face up (lets the lens fall back); and give analgesia and antiemetics.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the single most useful systemic IOP-lowering agent in AACG, and its cautions?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: IV/oral acetazolamide 500 mg (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) — it reduces aqueous production. Avoid in sulphonamide allergy and sickle cell disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What topical medical agents are used to lower IOP in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Topical beta-blocker (timolol — caution in asthma/COPD/bradycardia), topical alpha-2 agonist (brimonidine/apraclonidine), and topical steroid (prednisolone) to reduce inflammation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: When is IV mannitol used in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: As an osmotic agent if the IOP is not controlled by other measures.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is pilocarpine's action in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: A miotic — it constricts the pupil, pulling the iris away from the angle to reopen it.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Why must pilocarpine be timed carefully in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Because it only works once IOP is lowered: at very high IOP (>~40–50 mmHg) the iris sphincter is ischaemic and pilocarpine is ineffective, so it is given after IOP starts falling (defer if IOP >40).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the definitive treatment for AACG, and why is it done in both eyes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) — a small hole in the peripheral iris creates an alternative channel for aqueous to bypass the pupillary block, equalising pressure so the iris falls back and the angle reopens. Performed in BOTH eyes, as the fellow eye is predisposed (prophylaxis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is an increasingly used definitive alternative to LPI in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Lens extraction (cataract surgery) — especially where there is co-existing cataract.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What are the complications of untreated/delayed AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Permanent visual loss/blindness (optic nerve infarction), optic atrophy, central retinal artery or vein occlusion, recurrent attacks, and chronic angle-closure glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: How does AACG differ from primary open-angle glaucoma in presentation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: AACG: sudden onset, severe pain + headache, red congested eye, acute blurring with haloes, nausea/vomiting, fixed mid-dilated pupil, very high IOP. Open-angle: chronic/insidious, painless, white eye, gradual peripheral field loss, normal pupil, mildly-moderately raised IOP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A 28-year-old man presents with a painful, red, photophobic left eye, watering and blurred vision. There is circumcorneal (ciliary) redness, a small irregular pupil, and slit-lamp shows anterior chamber cells and flare with a hypopyon. He also has inflammatory back pain. What is the most likely diagnosis and association?
options: HLA-B27 anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: HLA-B27 anterior uveitis associated with ankylosing spondylitis
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: A young man with a painful, photophobic red eye, ciliary flush, a small irregular pupil, anterior chamber cells/flare and a hypopyon, plus inflammatory back pain, is the classic stem for HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis with ankylosing spondylitis. Hypopyon is characteristic of HLA-B27 and Behçet's disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: Which slit-lamp finding is the defining sign of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Anterior chamber 'cells and flare' — inflammatory cells plus protein producing a hazy/milky beam from breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier — is the defining slit-lamp sign of anterior uveitis. Keratic precipitates, hypopyon and posterior synechiae are additional signs.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: What is the first-line treatment for acute anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Acute anterior uveitis is treated with topical corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone acetate 1%, frequent then tapered) to suppress inflammation, plus a cycloplegic/mydriatic (cyclopentolate/atropine) to relieve pain from ciliary spasm and to prevent/break posterior synechiae. Antibiotics/antihistamines are not appropriate.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: Why is a cycloplegic (e.g. cyclopentolate) used in anterior uveitis, in addition to relieving pain?
options: To dilate the pupil and prevent/break posterior synechiae by keeping the iris off the lens
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: To dilate the pupil and prevent/break posterior synechiae by keeping the iris off the lens
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: A cycloplegic/mydriatic relieves pain by paralysing ciliary spasm and, importantly, dilates the pupil to prevent or break posterior synechiae (iris sticking to the lens), which otherwise risk an irregular pupil, iris bombé and glaucoma. It moves the iris off the lens.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A patient with anterior uveitis develops an irregular, festooned pupil because the iris has stuck to the lens. What is this, and what serious complication can follow?
options: Posterior synechiae; iris bombé leading to acute glaucoma
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Posterior synechiae; iris bombé leading to acute glaucoma
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Posterior synechiae (iris adhering to the lens) cause an irregular/festooned pupil and can block aqueous flow through the pupil, leading to iris bombé (the iris bows forward) and acute angle-closure-type glaucoma. This is why cycloplegics are used to prevent/break synechiae.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: Which set of conditions is classically associated with HLA-B27-positive acute anterior uveitis?
options: Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis is linked to the seronegative spondyloarthropathies: ankylosing spondylitis (commonest), reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. This rheumatology crossover is a major examinable point.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: How can anterior uveitis be distinguished from conjunctivitis using a light source?
options: In uveitis, shining light in the unaffected eye causes pain in the affected eye (consensual photophobia); conjunctivitis does not
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: In uveitis, shining light in the unaffected eye causes pain in the affected eye (consensual photophobia); conjunctivitis does not
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Consensual photophobia — pain in the affected eye when light is shone in the other eye — is characteristic of anterior uveitis (from ciliary muscle involvement) and helps distinguish it from conjunctivitis, which does not cause this. Uveitis also shows ciliary flush and cells/flare.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A child with ANA-positive oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is screened for eye disease even though the eyes look normal and are not painful. Why?
options: JIA uveitis is always painful and obvious
JIA-associated uveitis is typically chronic and painless ('white'), so it can silently cause complications and needs screening
Screening is only for red painful eyes
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: JIA-associated uveitis is typically chronic and painless ('white'), so it can silently cause complications and needs screening
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: JIA-associated uveitis is characteristically chronic and painless ('white' eye), so it does not present with the typical painful red eye and can silently progress to sight-threatening complications. ANA-positive oligoarticular children are therefore screened regularly with slit-lamp examination.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A patient with sarcoidosis-related uveitis is noted to have large greasy deposits on the corneal endothelium. What are these called and what do they suggest?
options: 'Mutton-fat' keratic precipitates; a granulomatous cause such as sarcoidosis
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: 'Mutton-fat' keratic precipitates; a granulomatous cause such as sarcoidosis
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Large, greasy 'mutton-fat' keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium suggest granulomatous uveitis, classically from sarcoidosis (also TB). Smaller KPs occur in non-granulomatous disease. This finding helps direct the systemic work-up (e.g. ACE, CXR).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: When is a systemic work-up warranted in anterior uveitis?
options: After every first, typical, mild episode
When it is recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, or accompanied by systemic features
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: When it is recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, or accompanied by systemic features
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: A first typical mild episode of anterior uveitis often needs no systemic work-up. Investigation (HLA-B27, ESR/CRP, ACE/CXR, syphilis/TB serology, ANA in children, spondyloarthropathy imaging) is warranted when it is recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, or has systemic features, guided by the history.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A patient with recurrent, sight-threatening uveitis is not controlled by topical steroids. Which treatment is appropriate, and under whose joint care?
options: Topical antibiotics alone by the GP
Systemic immunosuppression/biologics such as methotrexate or anti-TNF (adalimumab), with rheumatology
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Systemic immunosuppression/biologics such as methotrexate or anti-TNF (adalimumab), with rheumatology
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Chronic, recurrent or sight-threatening uveitis unresponsive to topical steroids is managed with periocular/systemic steroids and systemic immunosuppression or biologics (methotrexate, anti-TNF such as adalimumab), jointly with rheumatology, alongside treating any underlying systemic disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A patient with anterior uveitis develops gradually reduced central vision. Which complication is a common cause of visual loss in uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Cystoid macular oedema is a common cause of visual loss in uveitis, from inflammatory fluid accumulation at the macula. Other complications include posterior synechiae/glaucoma, cataract and band keratopathy. OCT helps detect macular oedema, and treatment targets the inflammation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A young man with a painful red eye and a hypopyon also gives a history of recurrent oral and genital ulcers. Which systemic diagnosis should be considered?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Uveitis with hypopyon plus recurrent oral and genital ulcers is characteristic of Behçet's disease. Hypopyon uveitis also occurs in HLA-B27-associated disease, but the mucocutaneous ulcer history points specifically to Behçet's, which requires systemic immunosuppression.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: Which pattern of redness helps distinguish anterior uveitis from conjunctivitis?
options: Diffuse redness greatest towards the fornices
Ciliary flush — circumcorneal injection concentrated around the limbus
A localised wedge of bright-red episcleral vessels
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Ciliary flush — circumcorneal injection concentrated around the limbus
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Anterior uveitis produces ciliary flush — circumcorneal (limbal) injection — whereas conjunctivitis causes diffuse redness that is greatest towards the fornices. The ciliary flush, together with photophobia, a small pupil and cells/flare, points to uveitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A patient with herpetic (HSV) anterior uveitis with raised intraocular pressure and iris atrophy needs treatment. What must be included?
options: Antiviral treatment (e.g. aciclovir) for the infective cause, alongside inflammation control
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Antiviral treatment (e.g. aciclovir) for the infective cause, alongside inflammation control
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Infective (herpetic) uveitis requires treatment of the underlying cause with antivirals (e.g. aciclovir), in addition to controlling inflammation and monitoring/treating the frequently raised IOP. Iris atrophy and raised IOP are clues to a herpetic cause.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: Which statement correctly contrasts anterior and posterior uveitis?
options: Anterior uveitis is a painful, red, photophobic eye; posterior uveitis is often painless and white, presenting with floaters and visual loss
Posterior uveitis is painful; anterior is painless
Anterior uveitis presents with floaters only
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Anterior uveitis is a painful, red, photophobic eye; posterior uveitis is often painless and white, presenting with floaters and visual loss
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Anterior uveitis (iris ± ciliary body) presents as a painful, red, photophobic eye with anterior chamber cells/flare, whereas posterior uveitis (choroid/retina) is often painless with a white eye, presenting with floaters and visual loss from vitritis and chorioretinal lesions. This site-based distinction guides assessment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A patient with anterior uveitis is treated with topical steroids. Which complications are recognised, including from the steroids themselves?
options: Cataract and glaucoma (uveitic or steroid-induced), plus synechiae and macular oedema
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Cataract and glaucoma (uveitic or steroid-induced), plus synechiae and macular oedema
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: Anterior uveitis can cause posterior synechiae (→ iris bombé/glaucoma), cataract and cystoid macular oedema, plus band keratopathy in chronic disease. Both cataract and glaucoma can also be induced by the topical steroids used to treat it, so IOP and lens changes are monitored during treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.question: A patient presents with a first, typical, mild episode of unilateral acute anterior uveitis with no systemic symptoms. What is the appropriate approach to investigation?
options: Extensive systemic work-up for all possible causes
Often no systemic work-up is needed; treat and reserve investigation for recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous or systemic cases
No treatment or investigation at all
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.answer: Often no systemic work-up is needed; treat and reserve investigation for recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous or systemic cases
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.explanation: A first, typical, mild episode of acute anterior uveitis often does not require a systemic work-up — it is treated with topical steroids and a cycloplegic. Investigation (HLA-B27, ACE/CXR, syphilis/TB, ANA, etc.) is reserved for recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous or systemically-associated disease, guided by the history.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A 30-year-old woman has a sectoral bright-red eye with mild gritty discomfort, normal vision and no photophobia. Phenylephrine drops cause the redness to blanch and the eye to whiten. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: A sectoral bright-red eye with minimal pain, normal vision, and vessels that BLANCH with phenylephrine is episcleritis — a benign, self-limiting condition. Blanching indicates the inflamed vessels are superficial (episcleral). In scleritis the deep scleral vessels do not blanch.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A 55-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis has a deep violaceous red eye with severe boring pain that wakes her at night and worsens on eye movement; the globe is tender. Phenylephrine does not blanch the redness. What is the diagnosis and required action?
options: Scleritis — urgent ophthalmology referral and systemic work-up
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Scleritis — urgent ophthalmology referral and systemic work-up
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Severe deep boring pain (worse at night and on eye movement), a violaceous globe that is tender, and vessels that do NOT blanch with phenylephrine indicate scleritis — a sight-threatening emergency. It requires urgent referral and a systemic work-up, especially given her rheumatoid arthritis (the commonest association).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: Which test is the key discriminator between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: The phenylephrine blanching test is the key discriminator: superficial episcleral vessels blanch (the eye whitens) in episcleritis, whereas the deep scleral vessels persist and do not blanch in scleritis. This distinguishes the benign condition from the sight-threatening one.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient is diagnosed with scleritis. Why is a systemic work-up mandatory?
options: About 50% of scleritis cases have an underlying systemic autoimmune/vasculitic disease, and it can be the first sign of life-threatening vasculitis such as GPA
Because scleritis is infectious in all cases
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: About 50% of scleritis cases have an underlying systemic autoimmune/vasculitic disease, and it can be the first sign of life-threatening vasculitis such as GPA
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Around half of scleritis cases are associated with systemic disease (commonly rheumatoid arthritis), and scleritis can be the presenting feature of life-threatening ANCA-associated vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. So a systemic work-up (ESR/CRP, ANCA, RF, ANA, urinalysis, etc.) with rheumatology is mandatory.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: What is the first-line drug treatment for non-necrotising scleritis?
options: Systemic NSAIDs (e.g. oral flurbiprofen or indomethacin)
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Systemic NSAIDs (e.g. oral flurbiprofen or indomethacin)
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Systemic NSAIDs (oral flurbiprofen or indomethacin) are first-line for non-necrotising scleritis. Systemic corticosteroids are used for severe/non-responsive disease, and immunosuppression/biologics for necrotising or vasculitic disease, under rheumatology, alongside treating any underlying systemic/infective cause.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is noted to have painless scleral thinning with visible underlying uvea, without inflammation. What is this called?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Scleromalacia perforans is necrotising scleritis WITHOUT inflammation — painless scleral thinning occurring in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, through which the darker uvea becomes visible. It contrasts with the intensely painful necrotising scleritis with inflammation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient presents with proptosis, pain on eye movement, disc swelling and reduced vision, but relatively little external redness. Which diagnosis should be considered and what confirms it?
options: Posterior scleritis — B-scan ultrasound showing the 'T-sign'
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Posterior scleritis — B-scan ultrasound showing the 'T-sign'
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Posterior scleritis (behind the equator) can cause proptosis, pain on movement, disc swelling and retinal/choroidal changes with little external redness, making it harder to diagnose. B-scan ultrasound showing the characteristic 'T-sign' (fluid in Tenon's space) confirms it.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: Which systemic condition is the COMMONEST association of scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is the commonest systemic association of scleritis. Other important associations include GPA/Wegener's and other ANCA-associated vasculitides, SLE, relapsing polychondritis, IBD, sarcoidosis and seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient with scleritis has haematuria and a raised creatinine, and ANCA is positive. Which underlying diagnosis is most likely and why does it matter?
options: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (an ANCA-associated vasculitis) — it is life-threatening and needs urgent immunosuppression
Rheumatoid arthritis with no systemic risk
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (an ANCA-associated vasculitis) — it is life-threatening and needs urgent immunosuppression
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: ANCA positivity with renal involvement (haematuria, raised creatinine) in a patient with scleritis points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a life-threatening ANCA-associated vasculitis for which scleritis may be the presenting feature. It requires urgent immunosuppression (e.g. cyclophosphamide/rituximab) under rheumatology — not to be missed.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: How does the nodule in nodular episcleritis differ from that in nodular scleritis?
options: The episcleritis nodule is mobile, whereas the scleritis nodule is immobile
The episcleritis nodule is immobile; the scleritis nodule is mobile
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: The episcleritis nodule is mobile, whereas the scleritis nodule is immobile
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: In nodular episcleritis the nodule is mobile (it can be moved over the sclera), whereas in nodular scleritis the nodule is immobile (fixed to the deeper sclera). This, along with pain severity and the phenylephrine test, helps distinguish the two.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient with a mildly uncomfortable, sectoral red eye and normal vision is diagnosed with a first, typical episode of episcleritis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassurance that it is self-limiting (~1–2 weeks), with lubricants for comfort and NSAIDs if troublesome
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Reassurance that it is self-limiting (~1–2 weeks), with lubricants for comfort and NSAIDs if troublesome
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: A single typical episode of episcleritis is benign and self-limiting (~1–2 weeks), managed with reassurance and lubricants, with topical/oral NSAIDs if troublesome. No systemic work-up is needed for a single typical episode; investigation is reserved for recurrent or atypical cases.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: Which feature most reliably points to scleritis rather than episcleritis?
options: Severe deep boring pain that wakes the patient at night and worsens on eye movement
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Severe deep boring pain that wakes the patient at night and worsens on eye movement
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Severe, deep, boring pain that wakes the patient at night and worsens on eye movement (as the extraocular muscles insert into the sclera) is characteristic of scleritis. Mild discomfort, salmon-pink redness, blanching vessels and a mobile nodule all point to episcleritis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient with severe necrotising scleritis and confirmed vasculitis requires treatment beyond NSAIDs. Which is most appropriate, and under whose care?
options: Topical steroids alone by the GP
Systemic immunosuppression/biologics (e.g. cyclophosphamide or rituximab) under rheumatology
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Systemic immunosuppression/biologics (e.g. cyclophosphamide or rituximab) under rheumatology
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Necrotising/vasculitic scleritis requires systemic immunosuppression or biologics (e.g. cyclophosphamide or rituximab) managed jointly with rheumatology, in addition to treating the underlying systemic disease. NSAIDs are first-line only for non-necrotising disease; topical steroids are merely adjunctive.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient with scleritis is being investigated for an underlying cause. Which test specifically screens for granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: ANCA testing screens for granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other ANCA-associated vasculitides — a key part of the scleritis work-up because scleritis can be the first sign of these life-threatening conditions. RF/anti-CCP relate to rheumatoid arthritis, ANA/anti-dsDNA to SLE, ACE to sarcoid, and HLA-B27 to spondyloarthropathies.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: Which statement about vision and urgency best contrasts episcleritis and scleritis?
options: Both threaten vision and are emergencies
Episcleritis has normal vision and is self-limiting; scleritis may reduce vision and is a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent referral
Episcleritis reduces vision; scleritis does not
Both are benign and need no referral
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Episcleritis has normal vision and is self-limiting; scleritis may reduce vision and is a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent referral
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Episcleritis has normal vision and is a benign, self-limiting condition, whereas scleritis may reduce vision and is a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent ophthalmology referral and a systemic work-up. This difference in visual risk and urgency is central to distinguishing them.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: A patient has a painful red eye and is about to be given topical steroids for presumed episcleritis, but the pain is severe and boring and the vessels do not blanch with phenylephrine. What should be done instead?
options: Proceed with topical steroids and reassure
Recognise this as scleritis and arrange urgent ophthalmology referral with systemic work-up
Patch the eye and review in a month
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.answer: Recognise this as scleritis and arrange urgent ophthalmology referral with systemic work-up
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Severe boring pain and non-blanching vessels indicate scleritis, not episcleritis, so instead of treating as a benign condition the patient needs urgent ophthalmology referral, systemic NSAIDs/steroids/immunosuppression as appropriate, and a systemic work-up for associated autoimmune/vasculitic disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.question: Which infective causes should be considered in the differential of scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.explanation: Although most scleritis is autoimmune/vasculitic, infective causes should be considered — herpes zoster, tuberculosis and syphilis (and gout as a crystal-related cause). The infection screen (syphilis, TB, HSV/VZV) is part of the work-up, and herpetic scleritis is treated with antivirals.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A 60-year-old myope reports a sudden shower of new floaters and flashing lights, followed by a dark curtain descending over the outer part of his vision, all painless. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: The painless triad of flashes, a sudden increase in floaters, and a descending 'curtain' across the visual field in a myope is classic rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. The curtain corresponds to the detached retina. It is a sight-threatening emergency requiring same-day ophthalmology referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A patient with a suspected retinal detachment is found to have an intact macula and normal central acuity. How does this affect the urgency of surgery?
options: It can be managed electively over weeks
It is extremely urgent — operate before the macula detaches to preserve central vision (ideally within ~24 hours)
No surgery is needed if the macula is on
Surgery should be delayed until the macula detaches
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: It is extremely urgent — operate before the macula detaches to preserve central vision (ideally within ~24 hours)
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: A 'macula-on' detachment (central vision still intact) is extremely urgent because operating before the macula detaches gives the best visual outcome (ideally within ~24 hours). While awaiting surgery, the patient is postured to keep subretinal fluid away from the macula. Once the macula detaches, central vision often does not fully recover.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: Which is the commonest type of retinal detachment, and what underlies it?
options: Rhegmatogenous — a retinal break/tear allowing vitreous fluid under the retina
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: Rhegmatogenous — a retinal break/tear allowing vitreous fluid under the retina
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (from a 'rhegma'/break) is the commonest type: a retinal tear lets vitreous fluid pass under the retina. It is associated with PVD, myopia, trauma and previous cataract surgery, and presents with the classic flashes/floaters/curtain.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: Which two factors are the key risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
options: Age under 20 and contact lens use
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Myopia (a longer, thinner eye/retina) is the biggest risk factor, and posterior vitreous detachment (the ageing vitreous pulling on the retina to cause a tear) is the key precipitant. Other risks include age, pseudophakia (previous cataract surgery), trauma and lattice degeneration.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A patient reports new flashes and floaters but has normal vision and no visual field defect. Examination shows a Weiss ring but no retinal tear. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate action?
options: Posterior vitreous detachment — benign, but assess to exclude a tear and safety-net for warning signs
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: Posterior vitreous detachment — benign, but assess to exclude a tear and safety-net for warning signs
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: A Weiss ring with flashes/floaters but normal vision and no field defect suggests posterior vitreous detachment, which is common and benign. However, PVD can cause a retinal tear, so a dilated examination is needed to exclude a break, with safety-netting to return urgently if a curtain/shadow or reduced vision develops.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: What is the key investigation to diagnose retinal detachment and determine macular involvement?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy is the key test — it shows the grey, elevated, mobile detached retina, identifies breaks/tears, and determines whether the macula is on or off (which drives urgency). B-scan ultrasound is used if the view is obscured; OCT can also assess macular involvement.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A diabetic patient with proliferative retinopathy develops a retinal detachment as fibrous tissue contracts and pulls the retina off. What type of detachment is this?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: This is a tractional retinal detachment, in which fibrous (fibrovascular) tissue from proliferative diabetic retinopathy contracts and pulls the retina off the RPE — without a retinal break. Management addresses the underlying disease (laser/vitrectomy), differing from the surgery for rhegmatogenous detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A patient with malignant hypertension develops a retinal detachment from fluid leaking under the retina, with no break or traction. What type is this and how is it primarily managed?
options: Exudative (serous) — treat the underlying cause (control the blood pressure)
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: Exudative (serous) — treat the underlying cause (control the blood pressure)
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Fluid leaking under the retina without a break or traction is an exudative (serous) detachment, seen with inflammation, tumours, malignant hypertension/pre-eclampsia and central serous retinopathy. It is managed by treating the underlying cause (e.g. controlling the blood pressure), rather than by the surgery used for rhegmatogenous detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: Which surgical procedure removes the vitreous, drains subretinal fluid, seals breaks and uses gas or silicone oil tamponade for a rhegmatogenous detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Pars plana vitrectomy removes the vitreous, drains subretinal fluid, seals the breaks and provides gas or silicone oil tamponade (with post-operative posturing), and is favoured for complex/posterior breaks, pseudophakia or vitreous haemorrhage. Scleral buckling and pneumatic retinopexy are alternative approaches.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A retinal TEAR (without detachment) is identified on dilated examination. What is the appropriate treatment to prevent detachment?
options: Laser retinopexy or cryotherapy to seal the break
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: Laser retinopexy or cryotherapy to seal the break
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: A retinal tear (break) without established detachment is treated with laser retinopexy or cryotherapy to seal the break and prevent fluid tracking under the retina and causing detachment. This is a key opportunity to prevent progression to a full detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A patient has a 'macula-off' retinal detachment with reduced central vision. How does this affect the timing and prognosis compared with macula-on?
options: It is no longer an emergency and can wait weeks
It is still urgent (ideally within ~2–3 days) but central vision is already compromised and may not fully recover
The prognosis is better than macula-on
It should be operated within 1 hour like a stroke
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: It is still urgent (ideally within ~2–3 days) but central vision is already compromised and may not fully recover
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Once the macula has detached ('macula-off'), central vision is already lost and often does not fully recover, so while repair is still urgent (ideally within ~2–3 days) the window is slightly less frantic than for macula-on. Macula-on detachments are operated within ~24 hours to preserve central vision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: What sign on slit-lamp examination, seen as pigment cells in the anterior vitreous, suggests a retinal tear?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Shafer's sign — pigment cells ('tobacco dust') in the anterior vitreous — suggests a retinal tear, as the break releases retinal pigment epithelial cells into the vitreous. Its presence with flashes/floaters raises concern for a tear/detachment and warrants careful dilated examination.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A patient has a suspected retinal detachment but the fundus view is obscured by a dense vitreous haemorrhage. Which investigation is most appropriate?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: When the fundus cannot be visualised (e.g. dense vitreous haemorrhage or cataract), B-scan ultrasound is used to detect a retinal detachment and assess its extent. Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy is preferred when the view is clear.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: A patient with new flashes and floaters develops a shadow across part of their vision. Why must they be referred urgently rather than reassured?
options: Flashes and floaters are always harmless
A curtain/shadow or reduced vision suggests a retinal tear or detachment rather than a benign PVD
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: A curtain/shadow or reduced vision suggests a retinal tear or detachment rather than a benign PVD
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: While isolated flashes and floaters may be a benign posterior vitreous detachment, the development of a curtain/shadow or reduced vision suggests a retinal tear or detachment, which is a sight-threatening emergency. The golden rule is that new flashes/floaters require assessment to exclude a break, and a curtain means urgent referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: While awaiting surgery for a macula-on retinal detachment, what interim measure helps protect central vision?
options: Positioning/posturing the patient to keep subretinal fluid away from the macula
Bilateral eye patching for a week
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: Positioning/posturing the patient to keep subretinal fluid away from the macula
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: While awaiting surgery, the patient is postured (position depending on the break location) to keep subretinal fluid away from the macula, helping to preserve central vision, and advised to avoid strenuous activity. Prompt surgery remains the definitive treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: Which of the following is a recognised surgical option that uses an intraocular gas bubble to tamponade a selected superior retinal break?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Pneumatic retinopexy injects an intraocular gas bubble to tamponade a selected superior break (combined with laser or cryotherapy), performed under local anaesthetic. Scleral buckling indents the sclera with a silicone band, and vitrectomy removes the vitreous — the choice depends on the break characteristics and lens status.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: Which patient is most at risk of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
options: A young hypermetrope with no eye history
A 65-year-old high myope who has had cataract surgery and now has posterior vitreous detachment
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: A 65-year-old high myope who has had cataract surgery and now has posterior vitreous detachment
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: High myopia, increasing age, pseudophakia (previous cataract surgery) and posterior vitreous detachment are all major risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, so a 65-year-old high myope who has had cataract surgery and now has a PVD is at particularly high risk and should be assessed promptly for any new flashes/floaters.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.question: Which statement best captures why retinal detachment is a time-critical emergency?
options: The eye becomes permanently red and painful
The detached neurosensory retina loses its RPE support, so photoreceptors die within days causing permanent visual loss if not repaired promptly
It rapidly spreads to the other eye
It causes immediate total blindness that is reversible
It only affects peripheral vision permanently
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.answer: The detached neurosensory retina loses its RPE support, so photoreceptors die within days causing permanent visual loss if not repaired promptly
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.explanation: Retinal detachment separates the photoreceptors from the RPE that nourishes them, so the detached retina loses its blood/nutrient supply and photoreceptors degenerate within days — leading to permanent visual loss if not repaired promptly. This, and the goal of operating before the macula detaches, make it a time-critical emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: A 58-year-old man has a routine fundoscopy showing generalised and focal arteriolar narrowing with AV nipping and copper wiring, but no haemorrhages or exudates. What Keith-Wagener-Barker grade is this?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Focal arteriolar narrowing with AV nipping and copper wiring, without haemorrhages/exudates, is Grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy. Grade 1 is mild generalised narrowing only; Grade 3 adds haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and exudates; Grade 4 adds papilloedema (malignant hypertension).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: A patient with a blood pressure of 210/130 has headache, blurred vision, and fundoscopy shows flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilloedema. What does this indicate and what is the priority?
options: Chronic grade 2 retinopathy — routine BP review
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Severe hypertension with retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilloedema is grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy = malignant (accelerated) hypertension, a medical emergency needing same-day specialist assessment/admission and assessment for other end-organ damage (AKI, heart failure, encephalopathy).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: When treating malignant hypertension with retinal changes, what is the key principle of blood pressure reduction?
options: Lower BP as fast as possible to normal
Lower BP gradually — by no more than about 25% in the first 24 hours
Do not treat the BP until the eye signs resolve
Only use oral medication over several weeks
Aim for a BP of 90/60 within an hour
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: Lower BP gradually — by no more than about 25% in the first 24 hours
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: In malignant hypertension, BP must be lowered gradually (by no more than ~25% in the first 24 hours), because rapid reduction risks cerebral, retinal and renal ischaemia/infarction. Controllable agents such as IV labetalol are used with monitoring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: What is the primary treatment for hypertensive retinopathy?
options: Controlling the blood pressure and cardiovascular risk
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: Controlling the blood pressure and cardiovascular risk
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: The treatment of hypertensive retinopathy is control of the blood pressure (and global cardiovascular risk) — it is not primarily an eye-directed treatment. Most retinal changes stabilise or improve with good BP control. Anti-VEGF/laser are for other retinal diseases.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: Which fundoscopic sign represents a nerve-fibre-layer microinfarct in hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Cotton-wool spots are fluffy white patches representing nerve-fibre-layer microinfarcts (ischaemia), seen in grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy (and also in diabetic retinopathy). Hard exudates are lipid/protein leakage; AV nipping and copper wiring reflect arteriosclerosis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: A patient with long-standing hypertension is found to have hard exudates arranged in a star pattern around the fovea. What is this called?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: A macular star is hard exudate (lipid/protein leakage) arranged radially around the fovea, seen in severe hypertensive retinopathy (and other conditions). It reflects the exudative phase of blood-retinal barrier breakdown and, with papilloedema, points to malignant hypertension.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: Why is examining the retina valuable in a hypertensive patient?
options: The retina is the only site where the effects of hypertension on blood vessels can be directly seen, and the grade reflects systemic cardiovascular/stroke risk
It measures the blood pressure directly
It replaces the need for BP measurement
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: The retina is the only site where the effects of hypertension on blood vessels can be directly seen, and the grade reflects systemic cardiovascular/stroke risk
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Fundoscopy allows direct visualisation of hypertensive vascular damage — the retina is the only place this can be seen directly — and the retinopathy grade correlates with cardiovascular, stroke and mortality risk. So it provides prognostic information about systemic vascular disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: A patient with hypertensive retinopathy suddenly loses vision in one eye. What should be suspected?
options: A retinal vein or artery occlusion, for which hypertension is a major risk factor
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: A retinal vein or artery occlusion, for which hypertension is a major risk factor
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Sudden visual loss in a hypertensive patient suggests a vascular complication such as a retinal vein or artery occlusion, for which hypertension is a major risk factor. Hypertensive retinopathy itself is usually asymptomatic, so new visual loss warrants urgent assessment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: Which set of features distinguishes hypertensive from diabetic retinopathy on fundoscopy?
options: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages and copper/silver wiring
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages and copper/silver wiring
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, copper/silver wiring and (in severe cases) papilloedema, whereas diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages and neovascularisation. Cotton-wool spots occur in both conditions.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: A young patient presents with severe, resistant hypertension and grade 3 retinopathy. What additional evaluation is important?
options: Screen for secondary causes of hypertension
Immediate laser treatment to the retina
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: Screen for secondary causes of hypertension
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Young age, severe or resistant hypertension warrants screening for secondary causes of hypertension (e.g. renal, endocrine). Alongside grading the retinopathy, assessment of other target-organ damage (renal via urinalysis/U&Es, cardiac via ECG/echo) is important.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: Which complication can result from prolonged papilloedema in malignant hypertension?
options: Optic atrophy with permanent visual loss
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: Optic atrophy with permanent visual loss
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Prolonged papilloedema in malignant hypertension can lead to optic atrophy and permanent visual loss. Other complications include retinal vein/artery occlusion, macular oedema/exudative retinal detachment, and worsening of any co-existing diabetic retinopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: A patient with grade 1–2 hypertensive retinopathy and no symptoms is managed how?
options: Manage hypertension per standard guidelines and address cardiovascular risk; most retinal changes stabilise/improve with good BP control
Immediate BP reduction to normal within an hour
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: Manage hypertension per standard guidelines and address cardiovascular risk; most retinal changes stabilise/improve with good BP control
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Chronic grades 1–2 hypertensive retinopathy is managed by treating the hypertension per standard guidelines (lifestyle plus antihypertensives) and addressing global cardiovascular risk (lipids, diabetes, smoking). Most retinal changes stabilise or improve with good BP control; emergency treatment is reserved for grade 4/malignant hypertension.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: Which sign in the Keith-Wagener-Barker classification marks the transition to malignant hypertension?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Papilloedema (optic disc swelling), which defines grade 4, marks malignant (accelerated) hypertension — a medical emergency. Copper wiring and AV nipping are grade 2 features, and haemorrhages/cotton-wool spots/exudates are grade 3; the addition of papilloedema is the critical transition.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: A patient with both diabetes and poorly controlled hypertension has worse retinopathy than expected. How does hypertension contribute?
options: Hypertension can worsen co-existing diabetic retinopathy, so BP control benefits both
Hypertension has no effect on diabetic retinopathy
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: Hypertension can worsen co-existing diabetic retinopathy, so BP control benefits both
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Hypertension worsens co-existing diabetic retinopathy, so good blood pressure control is an important part of managing diabetic eye disease (BP target <140/80, tighter with renal disease). Both conditions share vascular damage mechanisms and compound retinal injury.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.question: Which investigation set best supports the diagnosis and staging of hypertensive retinopathy and its systemic impact?
options: Blood pressure measurement and fundoscopy/dilated fundus exam, plus urinalysis/U&Es and ECG/echo for target-organ damage
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.answer: Blood pressure measurement and fundoscopy/dilated fundus exam, plus urinalysis/U&Es and ECG/echo for target-organ damage
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.explanation: Blood pressure measurement and dilated fundoscopy drive the diagnosis and grading, while urinalysis/U&Es (renal) and ECG/echo (LVH) assess other target-organ damage. Fundus photography/OCT/FFA aid documentation, and secondary hypertension is screened for in young/severe/resistant cases.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.question: A 40-year-old presents with a painful, watering, photophobic red eye. Slit-lamp with fluorescein shows a branching ulcer with terminal bulbs, and corneal sensation is reduced. What is the diagnosis and a key management rule?
options: Herpes simplex (dendritic) keratitis — topical antiviral, and topical steroids are contraindicated
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.answer: Herpes simplex (dendritic) keratitis — topical antiviral, and topical steroids are contraindicated
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.explanation: A branching dendritic ulcer that stains with fluorescein, with reduced corneal sensation, is pathognomonic of epithelial HSV keratitis. Treatment is topical antiviral (aciclovir 3% ointment or ganciclovir gel), and topical steroids are contraindicated because they promote viral replication and can cause a geographic ulcer and perforation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.question: Why must topical corticosteroids never be given for an undiagnosed painful red eye?
options: They can dramatically worsen epithelial HSV keratitis, enlarging the dendrite into a geographic ulcer with risk of perforation
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.answer: They can dramatically worsen epithelial HSV keratitis, enlarging the dendrite into a geographic ulcer with risk of perforation
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.explanation: In epithelial (dendritic) HSV keratitis, topical steroids promote viral replication, enlarging the dendrite into a geographic ('amoeboid') ulcer and risking corneal melt/perforation. This is why fluorescein must first exclude a dendritic ulcer — the classic reason never to give steroid drops for an undiagnosed red eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.question: Where does the herpes simplex virus lie latent before causing recurrent keratitis, and via which nerve does it reach the cornea?
options: Trigeminal ganglion; ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.answer: Trigeminal ganglion; ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve
